title: Number of 1 Bits
description:
Write a function that takes an integer and returns the number of 1 bits present in its binary representation.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ A ≤ 10^9

Input Format
First and only argument contains integer A.

Output Format
Return an integer.

Example Input
Input 1: 11
Input 2: 6

Example Output
Output 1: 3
Output 2: 2

Example Explanation
11 = 1011 (binary) → 3 set bits. 6 = 110 → 2 set bits.
story: Loop while A != 0. Add (A & 1) to count, then right-shift A by 1. Stop when A is 0.
plain: Two approaches: (a) bit-by-bit — repeatedly test LSB with (A & 1), add to count, shift A right; (b) Brian Kernighan — repeatedly do A = A & (A - 1) which clears the lowest set bit, count iterations. Both O(bits). Kernighan runs once per SET bit (faster on sparse numbers).
tale: A coin counter inspects a stack of coins in binary slots. She peeks at the lowest slot — if a coin sits there, she increments her tally — then slides the whole stack down one slot. She stops when the stack is empty.
pitfalls: If A could be negative, `N >> 1` keeps the sign bit and loops forever; use `>>>` instead.
Wrap the test as `(N & 1) == 1` with parens — `&` binds looser than `==`, so `N & 1 == 1` means the wrong thing.
Kernighan's `N & (N - 1)` only helps when N != 0; the `while` guard already handles the 0 case.

solutions.label: Bit-by-Bit
approach: While N != 0: if (N & 1) == 1, count++; N = N >> 1 (use >>> for unsigned in Java if negatives are possible).

solutions.label: Optimal — Brian Kernighan
solutions.plain: Loop while N != 0: N = N & (N - 1); count++. Each iteration removes one set bit.
solutions.tale: Snap off the lowest set coin each round.
approach: count = 0; while N != 0: N = N & (N-1); count++; return count.
solutions.story: Optimal — iterates once per set bit.

data.footer: Number of 1 bits — A = 29 = 11101₂. Bit-by-bit walk.

script.label: SETUP
script.msg: A = 29 = 11101₂. Bits shown MSB → LSB. Expected count = 4.
script.overlay: Bit order: position 0 = LSB. The displayed array reads MSB-first for readability.

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: Negative numbers: in Java, use >>> (unsigned right shift) so the sign bit doesn't propagate. Or use Integer.bitCount(A).

title: Single Number
description:
Given an array of integers A, every element appears twice except for one. Find that integer that occurs once.
NOTE: Your algorithm should have a linear runtime complexity. Could you implement it without using extra memory?

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ |A| ≤ 2 * 10^6
0 ≤ A[i] ≤ INTMAX

Input Format
The first and only argument of input contains an integer array A.

Output Format
Return a single integer denoting the single element.

Example Input
Input 1: A = [1, 2, 2, 3, 1]
Input 2: A = [1, 2, 2]

Example Output
Output 1: 3
Output 2: 1

Example Explanation
3 occurs once in input 1; 1 occurs once in input 2.
story: XOR is associative & commutative. x ^ x = 0. Folding XOR over the array cancels all pairs, leaving the lone element.
plain: XOR has two magical properties: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, and it's commutative. So XOR-folding the entire array makes every duplicated value cancel itself out, leaving only the unique number. One pass, O(N), O(1) memory.
tale: Twin coins in a sealed bag cancel each other's weight perfectly. After shaking the bag, only the single lonely coin's weight remains on the scale.
pitfalls: Start result at 0 (or A[0]) — starting anywhere else leaves a stray value XORed in.
This only works because every other number appears exactly twice; a triple would not cancel.
Values go up to INTMAX, so keep result as `int` and don't accidentally overflow into `long` math.

solutions.label: Brute — HashMap Count
solutions.plain: Count frequencies; return the one with count 1. Uses extra memory.
solutions.tale: Tally each coin; the loner has count 1.
approach: Build a frequency map; return the key with value 1.
solutions.pseudocode: freq map; return key with count == 1

solutions.label: Optimal — XOR Fold
solutions.plain: result = 0; for each v: result ^= v; return result.
solutions.tale: Twin coins cancel; the loner remains.
solutions.pseudocode: r = 0; for v in A: r ^= v

script.label: SETUP
script.msg: A = [4, 7, 2, 7, 4, 9, 2]. Every value pairs except 9. result = 0.
script.overlay: XOR laws: x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x, XOR is commutative & associative.

script.label: fold 2 → result=9 (2s cancelled)
script.msg: result = 11 ^ 2 = 9. Now 7s are also cancelled (4^4 = 0 elsewhere, 7^7 = 0 elsewhere).

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: Generalises: 'every value appears K times, except one appears once' can be solved with per-bit mod-K counting (see Single Number II).

title: Unset i-th Bit
description:
You are given two integers A and B. If B-th bit in A is set, make it unset. If B-th bit in A is unset, leave it as it is. Return the updated A value.
Note: The bit position is 0-indexed (LSB = index 0).

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ A ≤ 10^9; 0 ≤ B ≤ 30

Example
Input: A = 5, B = 2 → Output: 1 (101 → 001)
story: Mask = ~(1 << B). AND with A clears that bit, leaves others.
plain: Build mask = ~(1 << B). It has 0 at position B and 1 everywhere else. ANDing with A keeps every bit except position B, which becomes 0.
tale: A typist uses correction tape to blank out exactly one character — leaving every other character untouched.
pitfalls: Remember to complement: `A & (1 << B)` clears everything else, you want `A & ~(1 << B)`.
Watch precedence — keep the parens as `~(1 << B)`, since `~` and `<<` don't group the way you'd guess.
B can be up to 30, safe for int; if it ever hit 31 you'd need `1L` to avoid touching the sign bit.

solutions.label: Optimal

data.footer: Unset bit B=2 in A=13 (01101). Bit 2 is set → clear it.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Mask trick: isolate one bit, complement to get inverse mask.

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: Idempotent: unsetting an already-zero bit leaves the number unchanged.

title: Toggle i-th Bit
description:
You are given two integers A and B. If B-th bit in A is set, make it unset. If B-th bit in A is unset, make it set. Return the updated A value.
Note: bit position is 0-indexed.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ A ≤ 10^9; 0 ≤ B ≤ 30

Example
A = 4, B = 1 → 4 = 100; toggle bit 1 → 110 = 6.
A = 5, B = 2 → 5 = 101; toggle bit 2 → 001 = 1.
story: XOR with (1 << B) flips that bit, leaves others.
plain: XOR with the single-bit mask flips only the targeted bit. Because x ^ 1 = ~x and x ^ 0 = x, ANDing/XORing the mask only changes position B and leaves the rest alone.
tale: A light switch — press once: on becomes off, off becomes on. The other switches in the room stay where they are.
pitfalls: Use XOR here, not OR — OR can only turn a bit on, it never flips a 1 back to 0.
Toggling twice cancels out (`A ^ m ^ m = A`), so don't apply the mask an extra time by mistake.
B tops out at 30 so `1 << B` is fine; a bit-31 shift would land on the sign bit.

solutions.label: Optimal

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: XOR for toggle: single property — flips iff mask bit is 1.

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: Two toggles cancel: A ^ m ^ m = A. Useful when you need to revert a flip.

title: Check i-th Bit
description:
You are given two integers A and B. Return 1 if B-th bit in A is set, else 0.
Note: bit position is 0-indexed.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ A ≤ 10^9; 0 ≤ B ≤ 30

Example
A = 4, B = 1 → 100, bit 1 is 0 → 0.
A = 5, B = 2 → 101, bit 2 is 1 → 1.
story: AND with mask (1 << B); zero → bit unset (return 0), non-zero → bit set (return 1).
plain: Use AND with the single-bit mask. The result is either 0 (bit unset) or exactly (1 << B) (bit set). Compare for zero. A cleaner one-liner: return (A >> B) & 1.
tale: An inspector shines a torch on a single position. If the torch reflects, that bit is metal (set); if not, plastic (unset).
pitfalls: Compare against the mask, not 1: `A & (1 << B)` gives `1 << B` when set, not always 1.
The shortcut `(A >> B) & 1` is cleaner, but if A were negative you'd want `>>>`.
Parenthesize the mask compare — `A & (1 << B) == (1 << B)` without parens evaluates `==` first.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.tale: Probe the position with a mask.
approach: mask = 1 << B; if ((A & mask) != 0) return 1; return 0; OR simply return (A >> B) & 1.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Two equivalents: (A & (1< and (A >> B) & 1.

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: Useful in loops: walking bits with for B = 0..30: if ((A>>B)&1)… is the canonical pattern.

title: Set Two Bits (in 0)
description:
You are given two integers A and B. Set the A-th bit and B-th bit in 0, and return the result in decimal.
Note: bit positions are 0-indexed.

Problem Constraints
0 ≤ A ≤ 30; 0 ≤ B ≤ 30

Example
A = 3, B = 5 → 101000 = 40.
A = 4, B = 4 → 10000 = 16 (same bit set twice = once).
story: Start with 0; OR with (1 << A) and (1 << B). Setting same bit twice is idempotent.
plain: OR is the natural 'set bit' operation. Start with N = 0; N |= (1 << A); N |= (1 << B). When A == B, the second OR is a no-op (1 OR 1 = 1).
tale: Two switches in an empty fuse box. Flip A on, then flip B on. If they're the same switch, flipping it twice still leaves it on.
pitfalls: OR only turns bits on, so setting the same bit twice (A == B) is a no-op, not a doubling.
Start from 0, not some leftover value, or you'll set extra bits.
A and B go up to 30, safe for int; a 31 would push `1 << 31` onto the sign bit.

solutions.label: Optimal

data.footer: Set bits A=2, B=6 in 0. Result = 01000100 = 68.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: OR semantics: 1 OR x = 1, 0 OR x = x. So OR with a mask only TURNS BITS ON, never off.

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: If A == B, the second OR is a no-op — masks are idempotent under OR.

title: Find nth Magic Number
description:
Given an integer A, find and return the Ath magic number.
A magic number is defined as a number that can be expressed as a power of 5 or a sum of unique powers of 5.
First few magic numbers are 5, 25, 30 (5 + 25), 125, 130 (125 + 5), ...

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ A ≤ 5000

Input Format
The only argument given is integer A.

Output Format
Return the Ath magic number.

Example
A = 3 → 30. A = 10 → 650.
story: Magic numbers ↔ subsets of {5^1, 5^2, …}. The k-th subset is encoded by k's binary representation: bit i of k decides whether to include 5^(i+1).
plain: There's a bijection between positive integers k and subsets of {5^1, 5^2, …}: write k in binary, and for each bit-position i (starting at 0) that's set, include 5^(i+1). Walk the bits of A: if (A & 1) include 5^power; shift A right; power++.
tale: A jeweller orders rings by binary count. Ring #k is built from gold bands of weights 5, 25, 125, … picked according to which bits of k are set.
pitfalls: `Math.pow` returns a double — casting to int can round wrong for big powers; watch for precision.
5^power grows fast; for larger A the magic number can overflow int, so consider `long`.
Bump `power` and shift A every loop even for a 0 bit, or the power-to-bit alignment drifts.

solutions.label: Optimal — Binary Expansion of N
solutions.plain: Walk bits of A. For each set bit at index i, add 5^(i+1).
solutions.tale: Decode the binary of A as a subset over powers of 5.
approach: While A > 0: if (A & 1) == 1, magic += 5^power; A >>= 1; power++.
solutions.pseudocode:
magic = 0; pow = 1
while A: if A&1: magic += 5^pow; A >>= 1; pow++

data.footer: Find magic number for A=7 = 111₂. Expand bits → powers of 5.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Bijection: bit i of A (0-indexed) ↔ include 5^(i+1).

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: Why this bijection works: there are 2^k - 1 magic numbers using at most powers {5^1, .., 5^k}. Indexing them by binary of A enumerates subsets canonically.

title: Help From Sam
description:
Alex's score starts at 0. He can DOUBLE his score (free) or take a +1 boost from Sam. He wants score = A with minimum boosts from Sam.

Problem Constraints
0 ≤ A ≤ 10^9

Example
A = 5: 0 → +1=1 → ×2=2 → ×2=4 → +1=5 (2 boosts). A = 3: 0 → +1=1 → ×2=2 → +1=3 (2 boosts).
story: Reverse: divide A by 2 when even (free), subtract 1 when odd (one boost). Boosts = set-bit count of A.
plain: Reverse the process. From A, while A > 0: if A is even, halve it (free); if odd, subtract 1 (counts as one boost from Sam). The total subtractions equal the number of set bits in A — exactly popcount(A).
tale: Alex retraces his climb. Each time his score is even, he must have just doubled; halve it for free. Each time it's odd, his last move was a +1 from Sam — count it and shave one off.
pitfalls: The answer is just popcount(A) — don't overthink it into simulating the doubling forward.
A can be 0; the `while (N != 0)` loop correctly returns 0 boosts, so don't special-case it wrong.
Use `(N & 1) == 1` with parens, since `&` binds looser than `==`.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.tale: Sam-boost count = number of 1 bits in A.
approach: count = 0; while A != 0: if (A & 1) count++; A >>= 1; return count.
solutions.story: Optimal. Same code as 'Number of 1 Bits'.

data.footer: Help From Sam — A=12 = 1100₂. Set bits = 2 = boosts.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Why popcount? Binary digits encode the sequence of doubles & +1s — each '1' is a +1 step.

script.label: 12 even → halve to 6 (free)
script.msg: Last move was a double. Free. Now process 6 = 110.

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: Construction path: 0 → +1 → ×2 → +1 → ×2 → ×2 = 0,1,2,3,6,12.

title: Finding Good Days
description:
Boomer the cat: day d's stash = 2^(d-1) units. She eats only on 'good' days. Total she ate is A. How many good days?

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ A ≤ 2^31 - 1

Example
A = 5 = 4 + 1 = 2^2 + 2^0 → 2 good days (day 1 and day 3). A = 8 = 2^3 → 1 good day (day 4).
story: Each day = unique power of 2. Total A → unique sum of distinct powers of 2 → days = popcount(A).
plain: Each day's stash is a distinct power of 2. The total A has a unique binary representation, so the number of good days equals the count of set bits in A.
tale: The cat's diary, kept in binary, lists one entry per good day. The diary has as many entries as A has 1-bits.
pitfalls: A can be up to 2^31 - 1, so bit 30 is the top real bit; `N >> 1` on a positive int is fine here.
The answer is popcount(A) — each set bit is one good day, don't try to sum the powers.
Keep the mask test parenthesized as `(N & 1) == 1`.

solutions.label: Optimal
approach: Same as 'Number of 1 Bits': loop, AND with 1, shift right.

data.footer: Finding Good Days — A=21 = 10101₂. 3 set bits → 3 good days.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Mapping: bit i (LSB=day 1) set ⇒ Boomer ate on day i+1.

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: Unique decomposition: binary is the unique representation of a positive integer as a sum of distinct powers of 2.

title: Single Number II
description:
Every element appears thrice except one which occurs once. Find that element. O(N) time, O(1) memory expected.

Problem Constraints
2 <= |A| <= 5*10^6
0 <= A[i] <= INTMAX

Example
A = [1,2,4,3,3,2,2,3,1,1] → 4. A = [0,0,0,1] → 1.
story: For each bit position, sum '1's across all elements. The sum mod 3 = bit of the unique number. Reconstruct result one bit at a time.
plain: XOR alone fails because triples don't cancel (x ^ x ^ x = x). Instead, count set bits at each of the 32 positions across the array; for each position, the count mod 3 is exactly the corresponding bit of the lonely number (since triples contribute 0 mod 3). Reassemble the answer.
tale: Three identical jugglers and one stranger. For each costume colour, count torches lit. Triples leave a residue of zero modulo 3. Whatever residue remains belongs to the stranger.
pitfalls: Plain XOR fails here — `x ^ x ^ x = x`, so triples don't cancel; you must count per bit mod 3.
Loop all 32 bit positions, including bit 31, or you'll miss the sign bit of large values.
Compare `(A[j] & (1 << i)) == (1 << i)`, not `== 1`, since the masked result is `1 << i` when set.

solutions.label: Optimal — Bit Counting Mod 3
solutions.plain: For i = 0..31, count how many array elements have bit i set; if count % 3 == 1, set bit i in result.
approach: For i = 0..31: bitCount = 0; for each A[j]: if (A[j] >> i) & 1, bitCount++; if bitCount % 3 == 1, result |= (1 << i).
solutions.pseudocode: for bit i in 0..31: cnt = popcount at i; if cnt%3==1: result |= 1<<i

data.footer: Single Number II — per-bit mod-3 count. A = [6,6,6,7,5,5,5].

script.label: SETUP
script.msg: Find unique element. 6=110, 7=111, 5=101. Triples should cancel mod 3.
script.overlay: Why bit-by-bit: within each column, the count is (3×triplets) + lonelyBit. Mod 3 isolates lonelyBit.

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: Constant-space variant: use two integers ones, twos with a 3-state finite-state automaton — O(N) time, O(1) space, single pass.

title: Single Number III
description:
Given an array of positive integers A, two integers appear only once, all others appear twice. Find the two integers that appear only once (in ascending order).

Problem Constraints
2 <= |A| <= 100000; 1 <= A[i] <= 10^9

Example
A = [1,2,3,1,2,4] → [3,4]. A = [1,2] → [1,2].
story: XOR-fold whole array → x = a^b (the two unique numbers). x ≠ 0 so it has at least one set bit; partition array by that bit. XOR each partition → recovers a and b.
plain: XOR-fold the array → x = a XOR b, where a and b are the two uniques (all pairs cancel). Pick any set bit of x (LSB is easiest: lsb = x & -x). Partition the array into two groups: 'bit set' vs 'bit unset'. a and b fall into different groups (they differ at that bit), so XOR-folding each group cancels duplicates and yields a and b separately.
tale: Two stranger guests in a hall of twins. A scanner shines on every guest and flips a 'mystery flag' that ends up showing the XOR of just the two strangers' badges. Any flag-bit set means the strangers' badges differ there — so split the room by that bit and each subroom reveals one stranger.
pitfalls: `xorAll` is a ^ b, never 0 (the two uniques differ), so a set bit is guaranteed — but scan all 32 bits to find it.
Any single differing bit works to split the array; you don't need the lowest one specifically.
Compare against `(1 << magicIndex)`, not 1, when testing the partition bit.

solutions.label: Optimal — XOR Partition
solutions.plain: Fold XOR → x. Find a set bit. Partition array by that bit. Fold each half.
approach: x = XOR of all elements. (x = a ^ b.)
Find any set bit of x — call its position p.
Walk array: XOR into num1 if bit p set, else into num2.
solutions.pseudocode:
x = XOR all
p = lowest set bit of x
num1, num2 = 0, 0
for v: if (v>>p)&1: num1 ^= v else: num2 ^= v

data.footer: Single Number III — A = [10,7,5,7,3,5]. Uniques: 10 and 3.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Plan: XOR → set bit → partition → fold each side.

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: Trick: the LSB of xorAll can be isolated via x & -x in two's complement.

title: Subarrays with OR 1
description:
Binary array A of length N (each element 0 or 1). Count subarrays whose bitwise OR is 1.

Problem Constraints
1 <= N <= 10^4

Example
A = [0,0,1,1,0] → 11. A = [0,0,0] → 0.
story: OR = 1 means subarray contains at least one 1. Count complement: subarrays of all zeros, subtract from total.
plain: Direct count is tedious. Instead, count subarrays whose OR is 0 (entirely zeros) and subtract from N*(N+1)/2. For each maximal run of k consecutive zeros, k*(k+1)/2 subarrays sit entirely inside it.
tale: An auditor counts boxes containing at least one apple. He's lazy: he counts all boxes, then subtracts those containing only oranges (no apples).
pitfalls: Count the complement (all-zero runs) and subtract — counting OR=1 subarrays directly is messier.
Don't forget to flush the trailing zero run after the loop, or a run ending the array is dropped.
`N*(N+1)/2` for N up to 10^4 fits in int, but if N grew you'd want `long` to avoid overflow.

solutions.label: Optimal — Complement on Zero Runs
solutions.plain: Total subarrays = N*(N+1)/2. Walk A; tally zero-run length; on hitting a 1, add k*(k+1)/2 and reset. End by flushing.
approach: For each element: if 0 → zeroRun++; else → allZeroCount += zeroRun*(zeroRun+1)/2; zeroRun = 0.
solutions.pseudocode:
total = N(N+1)/2
for each: if 0: k++ else: allZero += k(k+1)/2; k=0
flush; return total - allZero

data.footer: Subarrays with OR=1 — A=[1,0,0,1,0,1]. Count all, subtract all-zero.

script.label: SETUP
script.msg: N = 6. Total subarrays = 6*7/2 = 21. Count all-zero subarrays, subtract.
script.overlay: Complement counting: when a predicate is hard to count directly, count its negation.

script.label: i=0: 1 → flush 0
script.msg: Zero run length 0. Nothing to add.

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: Why k*(k+1)/2: a run of length k has exactly that many contiguous subarrays inside it.

title: Subarray OR (Sum of ORs)
description:
Array A of size N. The value of a subarray = bitwise OR of all elements. Return sum of all subarray values mod 10^9+7.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ N ≤ 10^5; 1 ≤ A[i] ≤ 10^8

Example
A = [1,2,3,4,5] → 71. A = [7,8,9,10] → 110.
story: Sum of ORs = Σ over each bit b of (2^b * #subarrays where bit b appears at least once). Per bit: count zero-run subarrays as complement.
plain: Decompose: for each bit position b (0..26), count subarrays where at least one element has bit b set; multiply by 2^b; sum. For each bit, the count = totalSubarrays - subarraysWhereBitBIsAlwaysZero. The 'always zero' count comes from runs of consecutive elements where bit b is 0 (same k*(k+1)/2 trick as Subarrays with OR 1).
tale: An accountant adds revenue from 27 product columns. For each column, she counts how many monthly windows had at least one sale in that column; multiplies by column price; sums.
pitfalls: Use `1L << i` for the weight — `1 << i` is int and would overflow near bit 30.
Take mod at each step; the running sum over 27 bits and big counts easily overflows without it.
Flush the trailing zero run for every bit, and reset `zeroCount` after each set element.

solutions.label: Optimal — Per-Bit Complement
solutions.plain: For each bit, count zero-runs; subtract from totalSubarrays; multiply by 2^bit; sum mod 1e9+7.
approach: For each bit i = 0..26: zeroCount = 0, ignorable = 0.
Walk A: if (A[j] & (1<<i)) == 0, zeroCount++; else ignorable += zeroCount*(zeroCount+1)/2; zeroCount = 0.
contrib = (total - ignorable) * (1L << i) mod MOD. answer = (answer + contrib) mod MOD.
solutions.pseudocode: for each bit: count subarrays containing ≥1 elt with that bit set; weight by 2^bit

data.footer: Subarray OR sum — A=[1,2,4]. Per-bit contribution.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Bit independence: OR per bit is independent → sum contributions per bit.

script.label: Bit 0 set in: only A[0]
script.msg: Zero positions: A[1], A[2]. Zero runs after split: 0 (before A[0]) | 2 (after). Ignorable = 0 + 2*3/2 = 3. Bit-0 subarrays = 6-3 = 3. Contribution = 3 * 1 = 3.

script.label: Bit 1 set in: only A[1]
script.msg: Zero runs around: 1 (A[0]) and 1 (A[2]). Ignorable = 1+1 = 2. Subarrays = 4. Contribution = 4 * 2 = 8.

script.label: Bit 2 set in: only A[2]
script.msg: Zero runs around: 2 (A[0..1]) and 0. Ignorable = 3. Subarrays = 3. Contribution = 3 * 4 = 12.

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: Why 27 bits: A[i] ≤ 10^8 < 2^27, so bits 0..26 cover everything.

title: Find Two Missing Numbers
subTopic: XOR Partition (a la Single Number III)
description:
Array A of length N has distinct elements from range [1, N+2]. Two numbers are missing. Find both (sorted).

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ N ≤ 10^5

Example
A = [3,2,4] → [1,5]. A = [5,1,3,6] → [2,4].
story: XOR all 1..N+2, XOR all A; the result is m1 ^ m2 (the two missing). Then 'Single Number III' partition recovers each.
plain: Same trick as Single Number III, but the 'universe' is implicit. Compute X = XOR(1..N+2) ^ XOR(A) — this equals m1 ^ m2 because every element in A cancels its mate in the range; only the two missing remain. Pick any set bit of X, partition both the range and the array by that bit, fold each partition. The two folds give m1 and m2.
tale: Two tickets are missing from a numbered raffle drum. The auditor XORs every ticket number 1..N+2 against every ticket in the drum — what survives is the XOR of the two absent tickets, then the partition trick recovers each.
pitfalls: X = xorRange ^ xorArr is m1 ^ m2 and never 0, so a set bit exists — but loop all 32 bits to find it.
Partition BOTH the range 1..N+2 and the array A by the same bit; folding only one side won't work.
Compare with `(1 << p)`, not 1, and remember the range goes to N+2, not N.

solutions.label: Optimal — XOR Partition (range vs array)
solutions.plain: X = XOR(1..N+2) ^ XOR(A). Pick a set bit p of X. Partition both the range AND A by bit p; XOR each partition. Combine to get m1 and m2.
approach: xorRange = XOR of 1..N+2. xorArr = XOR of A. X = xorRange ^ xorArr (= m1 ^ m2).
Find a set bit p of X.
Build allSet = XOR of i in 1..N+2 with bit p set; arrSet = XOR of v in A with bit p set.
num1 = allSet ^ arrSet. num2 = (allSet ^ xorRange) ^ (arrSet ^ xorArr) (the bit-unset partition).
solutions.pseudocode:
X = xorRange ^ xorArr
pick bit p of X
fold range/array by p → 4 folds → recover m1, m2

title: Min XOR value
description:
Given an integer array A of N integers, find the pair of integers in the array which have minimum XOR value. Report the minimum XOR value.

Problem Constraints
2 <= length of the array <= 100000
0 <= A[i] <= 10^9

Input Format
First and only argument of input contains an integer array A.

Output Format
Return a single integer denoting minimum xor value.

Example Input
Input 1: A = [0, 2, 5, 7]
Input 2: A = [0, 4, 7, 9]

Example Output
Output 1: 2
Output 2: 3
story: Two numbers XOR to a small value only when they share a long leading-bit prefix — and the most-similar numbers sit next to each other once sorted. So sort, then take the min XOR over ADJACENT pairs only: O(N log N) instead of O(N^2).
plain: Brute-forcing all pairs is O(N^2). Key fact: the minimum-XOR pair is always adjacent after sorting, because for sorted a <= b <= c the middle b shares at least as many high bits with each neighbour as the neighbours do with each other, so a^c can never beat both a^b and b^c. Sort A, then scan adjacent pairs tracking the minimum.
tale: Line people up by height; the two most alike are always standing shoulder to shoulder — no need to compare across the whole room.
pitfalls: Don't compare all pairs (O(N^2) TLE at N=1e5) — only adjacent pairs after sorting.
XOR of two ints up to 1e9 fits in int, but if you accumulate/sum XORs use long.
Duplicates give XOR 0, the global minimum — you can early-exit when minXor hits 0.

solutions.label: Optimal — Sort then Adjacent XOR
solutions.plain: Sort, then the answer is the smallest XOR among neighbouring elements.
approach: Slide a size-2 window (start,end): for each adjacent pair, minXor = min(minXor, A[start]^A[end]); early-exit if it reaches 0.
solutions.pseudocode:
sort(A)
min = A[0]^A[1]
for i in 1..N-2: min = Math.min(min, A[i]^A[i+1])
return min
solutions.story: Correctness rests on the leading-bit argument: the minimum can't 'jump over' an intermediate sorted value.

data.footer: Min XOR = min over adjacent pairs after sorting.

title: Strange Equality
description:
Given an integer A. Two numbers, X and Y, are defined as follows:
- X is the greatest number smaller than A such that the XOR sum of X and A is the same as the sum of X and A.
- Y is the smallest number greater than A, such that the XOR sum of Y and A is the same as the sum of Y and A.

Find and return the XOR of X and Y.

NOTE 1: XOR of X and Y is defined as X ^ Y where '^' is the BITWISE XOR operator.
NOTE 2: Your code will be run against a maximum of 100000 Test Cases.

Problem Constraints
1 <= A <= 10^9

Input Format
First and only argument is an integer A.

Output Format
Return an integer denoting the XOR of X and Y.

Example Input
Input 1: A = 5

Example Output
Output 1: 10
story: The whole trick is one identity: X + A == X ^ A exactly when X & A == 0 (no shared set bits → no carries). So X = flip every bit of A within its bit-length (the largest value < A with no overlap), and Y = 1 << (bit-length of A) (the next power of two above A's top bit, the smallest value > A with no overlap). Answer = X ^ Y.
plain: Addition equals XOR only when there are no carries, i.e. the two operands share no set bit (X & A == 0). To get the GREATEST X < A with X & A == 0, take the complement of A restricted to A's bit-length — set exactly the bits A leaves unset below its MSB. To get the SMALLEST Y > A with Y & A == 0, use the first bit position beyond A's highest set bit: Y = 1 << numberOfBits(A). Return X ^ Y.
tale: Two dancers can only 'add cleanly' if they never step on the same tile (no shared 1-bits). X fills every empty tile below A's top; Y takes the first fresh tile just above it.
pitfalls: The identity is a + b == a ^ b  ⇔  a & b == 0 (equivalently no carry). Memorise it — it unlocks the whole problem.
checkIfIthBitIsSet must compare to the mask, not to 1: (num & (1<<pos)) == (1<<pos), NOT == 1 (that only works for pos 0).
numberOfBits(A) = floor(log2(A)) + 1; guard A limits so 1 << numberOfBits doesn't need more than 31 bits (A <= 1e9 → up to 30 bits, safe in int).

solutions.label: Optimal — Complement Below MSB, Next Bit Above
solutions.plain: X = A with every bit flipped inside its bit-length; Y = 1 << numberOfBits(A). Return X ^ Y.
approach: numberOfBits = floor(log2(A)) + 1; Y = 1 << numberOfBits (smallest number > A sharing no bit with A).
Build X from A: for each bit i in [0, numberOfBits): if A has bit i set, unset it in X; else set it. This yields the greatest X < A with X & A == 0.
solutions.pseudocode:
nb = floor(log2(A)) + 1
Y = 1 << nb
X = A; for i in 0..nb-1: X = A.bit(i)? unset(X,i) : set(X,i)
return X ^ Y
solutions.story: Rests on: X + A == X ^ A  iff  X & A == 0. X is the in-length complement, Y is the next higher power of two.
